title: From Adam to Noah: The Book of Generations
summary: The chapter traces ten generations from Adam to Noah, giving for each man his age when his son was born, the years he lived afterward, and his total lifespan, ending again and again with the words and then he died. One man breaks the pattern: Enoch walked with God and was taken away. The list ends with Lamech naming his son Noah in hope of relief from the cursed ground, and with Noah's three sons.
story: Chapter 4 ended with two lines: Cain's, which grew in skill and violence, and Seth's, where people began to call on the LORD. Chapter 5 follows Seth's line from Adam to Noah, the man through whom God will carry humanity through the flood. The chapter looks like a list, but it carries the story forward in two ways. It shows that God's blessing to be fruitful and multiply is still at work after the fall, since each man has sons and daughters. And it shows that the sentence of death spoken in the garden is also at work, since each man, however long he lives, dies. The line is carrying the promise of the woman's seed toward Noah.
historical:
The heading in verse 1, This is the book of the generations of Adam, is the only one of Genesis's section headings to use the word book, and some scholars take it as the title of an older written record that the author used. The list covers the time before the flood, which cannot be dated from outside sources. Adding the ages at which each man fathered his son, the Hebrew text gives 1,656 years from Adam's creation to the flood. The ancient Greek translation (the Septuagint) and the Samaritan Pentateuch (the Torah as preserved by the Samaritan community) give different figures for several of the fathers, so that the total is more than two thousand years in the Greek and fewer in the Samaritan. The differences show that ancient copyists already found these numbers significant and puzzling.

The Sumerian King List, a Mesopotamian document known from copies of the early second millennium BC, names a series of kings who reigned before the flood for vastly longer periods, some for tens of thousands of years each. Genesis shares the conviction that the earliest generations lived far longer than later ones, but its figures are far smaller, its men are not kings, and each of them dies.
cultural:
Genealogies mattered enormously in the ancient world. They established who belonged to a family, who could inherit, and how a people was connected to its past. The phrase became the father of does not always mean the next generation in Hebrew usage; it can mean became the ancestor of, and later biblical genealogies sometimes skip generations (Matthew 1:8 passes over three kings between Joram and Uzziah). Whether Genesis 5 has gaps is debated, since the precise ages at fatherhood seem to link each name to the next.

Names carried meaning. Lamech names his son Noah, which sounds like the Hebrew word for rest, and explains it with a related verb meaning comfort: “May this one comfort us in the labor and toil of our hands caused by the ground that the LORD has cursed” (verse 29). He is quoting the language of 3:17, where the ground was cursed and man's work became toil. A father hopes his son will bring relief from the curse. That hope will be answered in a way Lamech could not have imagined.
literary: The chapter is built on a formula repeated ten times with small variations: when X had lived so many years he became the father of Y; X lived so many years more and had other sons and daughters; all the days of X were so many years, and he died. The repetition is the point. By the eighth time, a reader hears the refrain and then he died as a drumbeat. That is why the two breaks in the pattern stand out. With Enoch the formula changes twice: he walked with God, and instead of dying he was no more, because God had taken him away. With Lamech the formula pauses for a spoken hope. The list also invites comparison with Cain's line in chapter 4. Several names are similar (Enoch, Lamech, and names close to Cain, Irad, Mehujael, and Methushael), and the seventh from Adam in each line forms a sharp contrast: Cain's Lamech boasts of killing, while Seth's Enoch walks with God. Critical scholars often see two versions of one ancient list; others see a deliberate pairing that sets two kinds of humanity side by side.

outline.t: Humanity created in God's likeness and blessed
Adam fathers Seth in his own image
Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, and Jared
Enoch walks with God and is taken
Lamech names Noah in hope of comfort

doctrines.note: The chapter opens by repeating that God created humanity in his likeness, male and female, and blessed them. Adam then fathers a son in his own likeness and image. The image of God is not lost after the fall; it is passed down through every generation, even as sin and death are passed down with it.

The refrain and then he died shows that the warning of 2:17 was not idle. Death now reigns over every generation, no matter how long the life. The genealogy is a quiet but relentless picture of the fall's consequences.

Two moments of hope break through the pattern of death. Enoch walks with God and does not die, a sign that death does not have the last word for those who belong to God. And Lamech names his son in hope of comfort from the curse, a longing the rest of Scripture will take up.

words.note: Halakh, to walk, used here in a special form in the phrase walked with God (verses 22 and 24). The same expression is used of Noah in 6:9. It describes a whole life lived in close fellowship with God, not a single act. Later the Bible uses walking as its most common picture for how a person lives before God.

Laqach, to take. It is an ordinary verb, but it becomes striking in verse 24: God had taken him away. The same verb is used when Elijah is taken up to heaven (2 Kings 2:3-10). The text does not explain where Enoch went, only that his life ended in God's presence without the refrain of death.

Nacham, to comfort, or in other forms to be sorry or relent. Lamech uses it in naming Noah. In a painful irony, the next chapter uses the same verb when the LORD regrets that he made humankind (6:6-7). The man named for comfort will live through God's grief over the world.

Demut, likeness, the word that stood beside image in 1:26. Verse 1 recalls that God made humanity in his likeness, and verse 3 says Adam fathered Seth in his own likeness. The two verses together show the image passed down through human generations, carrying both dignity and a fallen nature.

christ: Luke's Gospel traces Jesus' ancestry back through this very list and ends it with “the son of Enosh, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God” (Luke 3:38). Luke sets Jesus within the whole human family, not only within Israel, and presents him as the new head of that family. The chapter's refrain of death also frames the New Testament's hope. Paul says that death reigned from Adam until Moses (Romans 5:14), and that “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:26), an enemy Christ defeats by his resurrection. Enoch, who was taken without dying, is remembered in Hebrews 11:5 as one who pleased God by faith, and Jude calls him “the seventh from Adam” (Jude 1:14). His story is not a prophecy of Christ, but it is an early sign that God's purpose for those who walk with him reaches beyond the grave. Lamech's longing for someone to bring comfort from the curse is also a longing the New Testament sees answered in Christ, though that is a thematic link rather than a prediction.

hard.q: Did people before the flood really live for nine hundred years?
hard.a:
Readers who take Scripture with equal seriousness answer this in different ways. Many take the ages as literal, pointing out that the chapters that follow show lifespans falling steadily after the flood (Genesis 6:3, and the shorter lives in chapter 11), which suggests a real change in the human condition. Others think the numbers follow an ancient convention for honoring ancestors, perhaps shaped by numerical patterns or symbolism, and note that Mesopotamian lists used even larger numbers for the same era. Some suggest the numbers carry theological meaning, for example that Enoch's 365 years match the days of a solar year and that Lamech's 777 echo the sevens of chapter 4.

A related question is whether the genealogy can be used to date creation. In the seventeenth century Archbishop James Ussher added up the biblical figures and placed creation in 4004 BC, a date once printed in the margins of many English Bibles. Others argue that Hebrew genealogies can skip generations and were not written to be added up. What the chapter clearly teaches does not depend on settling this: God's blessing continues through human generations, death reigns because of sin, and God keeps a line of faith alive.

questions: Enoch is remembered not for what he built or achieved but because he walked with God. What would it mean for that to be the summary of your life?
The refrain and then he died repeats eight times. How does facing the reality of death change the way you think about how you spend your years?
Lamech named his son in hope that he would bring comfort from the hardship of work. What hopes do you place on the next generation, and which of them only God can fulfill?
